author: David Lassen
title: Port of Coos Bay receives $11.25 million grant for ship-to-rail terminal project - NewsBreak
text:
By David Lassen ,
1 days ago The port-owned Coos Bay Rail Line would haul traffic from the Port of Coos Bay’s planned container terminal to a connection with Union Pacific. Port of Coos Bay COOS BAY, Ore. — The Oregon International Port of Coos Bay has received an $11.25 million federal grant to improve rail infrastructure as part of its ongoing effort to develop a ship-to-rail container terminal and create a new West Coast gateway for intermodal traffic.
The grant announced Monday, April 27, comes from the U.S. Maritime Administration’s Port Infrastructure Development Program. It will improve rail infrastructure on the North Spit of Coos Bay to prepare the planned terminal area of the Pacific Coast Intermodal Port for cargo movement and improve connections to the Coos Bay Rail Line.
“This award sends a clear message that serious infrastructure in rural Oregon matters and that the South Coast has a real role to play in the state’s economic future,” Kyle Stevens, president of the Coos Bay Port Commission, said in a press release . “It reflects ongoing public support for practical investments that create jobs, expand opportunities for producers, and strengthen infrastructure with growing national significance.”
The project previously received a federal INFRA grant of $25 million and a $29.8 million Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvement Grant in 2024 [see “Announcement of 2024 CRISI grants begin,” Trains.com, Oct. 25, 2024]. The Oregon legislature approved $100 million in project funding last year [see “Coos Bay intermodal port project …,” July 3, 2025].
The project would see containers move by rail to interchange with the Union Pacific in Eugene, Ore., via the port’s 134-mile Coos Bay Rail Line. The new 175-acre container terminal, developed through a partnership of the port and Kansas City-based NorthPoint Development, has a projected capacity of 2 million TEUs, or 20-foot-equivalent units, the standard measure of international containers. The port would serve as a point of entry for imported goods, while also providing empty containers that can be used for outbound shipments of agricultural and other products.
The total cost of the project, which also involves deepening the port channel, is currently estimated at $2.3 billion. More information is available at the project website .
